The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Ukrainian President Zelensky says he's willing
to hold elections if President Trump can get Russia
to suspend its attacks on Ukraine for 60 days.
Terry Schultz reports Zelensky also weighed in
on Trump's deal to import Russian diesel fuel.
Addressing the annual Warsaw Security Forum conference,
President Zelensky said while holding elections
during a war would require changing Ukrainian law,
it would be possible if Russian attacks ceased
so that people could safely take part in the process.
He's heard here through an interpreter.
And it's also impossible now because of our military,
more than a million people who must vote,
but how will they vote while being on the front line?
Zelensky also suggested that instead of buying diesel
from Russia, the U.S. should buy from Ukraine.
He said he'd been given no advance notification
of the agreement with the Kremlin
that Trump announced Friday.
For NPR News, I'm Terry Schultz in Warsaw.
Israel's Supreme Court is ordering officials
to plan for the return of Palestinians to their homes
in the occupied West Bank.
NPR's Daniel Estrin says tens of thousands of Palestinians
have been displaced from their communities
for more than a year.
The Israeli Supreme Court has ordered the Israeli military
to specify a timeline for when Palestinian civilians
can return to their homes in several West Bank refugee camps.
Israel evacuated and largely destroyed those areas
during a military operation more than a year and a half ago.
Israel said it was countering militant strongholds.
It's the largest mass displacement in the West Bank
in many decades.
Infrastructure still hasn't been rebuilt
and families haven't been allowed to return.
An Israeli cabinet minister is calling
to ignore the court ruling.
Faisal Salama, the Palestinian leader
of one displaced refugee camp,
called the court ruling useless
as long as the Israeli military
continues to occupy the area.
Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
Many leaders of Native American tribal nations
are raising concerns about the Trump administration's proposal
for unprecedented changes to the next U.S. census.
It would reshape voting maps
and determine how federal funding
is distributed across the country.
And Pirasansi Lawang has more.
One proposed change is not to use the 2030 census
to produce statistics about race and ethnicity.
The topic has been part of the U.S. headcount
since the first one in 1790.
Trump officials say they see a, quote,
reduced need for that information,
which is used for redistricting
and enforcing civil rights laws.
Meghan Bishop of the National Congress of American Indians
is an enrolled citizen of the native village
of Afognac in Alaska.
There's a significant concern
about how federal funding would be distributed
through grants and other programs to tribes
if that race-ethnicity census question is erased.
The public can comment on their proposal
through November 2nd.
Hansi Lawang, NPR News.
U.S. futures contracts are trading flat at this hour.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The United States is in the midst
of the biggest and deadliest measles epidemic in decades.
With cases reported across the country,
infectious disease experts say some vaccinated adults
should consider getting another measles shot.
And Piras Maria Godoy has more.
Before vaccines, measles used to kill
four to 500 people in the U.S. each year.
Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine
is 97% effective.
Most people vaccinated before 1989
probably received just one dose
instead of the two doses recommended for children today.
Dr. Larry Kociolek of Northwestern University
says traditionally, one dose has been considered
sufficient protection for adults not at high risk,
but he says these days.
If you are living in areas with high measles activity,
it does make a whole lot of sense for adults
to go ahead and get that second dose.
If you're not sure of your vaccination history,
he says there's no harm in getting an extra dose
of the MMR vaccine.
Maria Godoy and PR News.
Cleanup continues in the Southeast
after Isaias came ashore in Florida on Friday.
The storm is blamed for at least four deaths.
More than 100,000 customers are still without power
in Alabama and Florida,
but that's down from around 700,000 out over the weekend.
Meanwhile, the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel
are still bringing the chance of heavy rain
over the Southwest today.
The National Weather Service has issued flash flood
advisories and watches for parts of several states.
I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News in Washington.
